ai_overview.text:
Eczema is a group of chronic, inflammatory skin conditions that cause dry, red, and intensely itchy skin.
Symptoms
- Intense itchiness (pruritus) that often worsens at night
- Dry, scaly, or cracked skin
- Red to brownish-gray patches, commonly on the hands, feet, ankles, wrists, neck, upper chest, eyelids, and inside the bends of the elbows and knees
- Small, raised bumps that may leak fluid and crust over when scratched
Causes and Triggers
- Genetics: A family history of eczema, asthma, or hay fever increases risk.
- Immune System: An overactive immune response to environmental elements.
- Skin Barrier: A defect in the skin barrier that lets moisture out and irritants in.
- Triggers: Stress, dry air, sweat, wool or synthetic fabrics, soaps, fragrances, and allergens like dust mites or pet dander.
Treatment and Management
- Moisturizing: Apply thick creams or ointments daily, ideally right after a short, warm bath or shower while the skin is still damp.
- Avoiding Irritants: Use gentle, fragrance-free cleansers and avoid known triggers.
- Medications: Over-the-counter or prescription topical anti-inflammatory creams (such as corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors), and biologic therapies for severe cases.

ai_overview.text:
You can lower your cholesterol by eating a heart-healthy diet, exercising regularly, and maintaining a healthy weight.
Heart-Healthy Eating
- Eat more soluble fiber: Foods like oatmeal, beans, lentils, Brussels sprouts, apples, and pears block cholesterol absorption in your digestive tract.
- Choose healthy fats: Replace saturated fats (butter, lard, and fatty meats) with unsaturated fats found in olive oil, avocados, nuts, and seeds.
- Eat omega-3 fatty acids: Salmon, mackerel, sardines, and flaxseeds support heart health and help lower triglycerides.
- Limit processed foods: Cut back on sugary drinks, trans fats, and ultra-processed baked goods.
Lifestyle Changes
- Get regular exercise: Aim for about 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity, like brisk walking or cycling, every week to raise good HDL cholesterol and lower bad LDL.
- Lose extra weight: Shedding even 5% to 10% of your body weight can improve your overall cholesterol profile.
- Quit smoking and limit alcohol: Stopping smoking raises HDL levels, while reducing alcohol keeps triglycerides in check.
Medical Options
- Talk to your doctor: If lifestyle changes are not enough, your doctor may recommend medications like statins or ezetimibe to manage your levels safely.
You can read more guidance from the Mayo Clinic, the New Zealand Heart Foundation, or Cos Cardiology.
